questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless indurated ulcer on his right forearm with surrounding satellite nodules and lymphangitis tracking up to the axilla. There is no fever. KOH mount shows cigar-shaped budding yeast cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) classically presents with a sporotrichoid pattern: a primary inoculation lesion followed by nodules along lymphatics. KOH/culture shows 'cigar-shaped' yeast cells. Trauma from plants (rose thorns, sphagnum moss) is the typical exposure.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple painless perianal condyloma-like lesions. Biopsy shows koilocytes with large nuclei and perinuclear halos. The lesion is found to contain HPV type 16. What is the most important next step?
opts: High-resolution anoscopy to rule out anal intraepithelial neoplasia
questions.exp: HPV 16 is a high-risk oncogenic type. In HIV-positive patients, anal HPV 16 infection carries high risk of progression to anal squamous cell carcinoma via anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN). High-resolution anoscopy with biopsy is essential to detect and grade AIN.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops tense blisters on normal-appearing skin and mucous membranes. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. The blister on electron microscopy is sublamina densa. Which antibody target is most characteristic?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) features autoantibodies against type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils), located in the sublamina densa. DIF shows linear IgG at BMZ. Unlike bullous pemphigoid (BP180, sublaminal lucida), EBA blisters are sub-lamina densa on EM.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 2 cm pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia on his nose. He has a long history of sun exposure. There is central ulceration. What is the most common histological subtype?
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma is the most common subtype (~60-70%), typically presenting as a pearly translucent nodule with overlying telangiectasia, commonly on the nose or cheeks. Central ulceration gives the classic 'rodent ulcer' appearance.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with tuberculoid leprosy is started on dapsone monotherapy. After 3 weeks he develops haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. The physician wants to add rifampicin. What is the rationale for adding rifampicin to dapsone in paucibacillary leprosy?
opts: Rifampicin is bactericidal against M. leprae while dapsone is bacteriostatic
Rifampicin prevents dapsone resistance in M. leprae
Rifampicin covers secondary bacterial infections in leprosy ulcers
questions.exp: Rifampicin is the only bactericidal drug against M. leprae (single dose kills 99.9% of viable bacilli). Dapsone is bacteriostatic. The combination ensures rapid elimination of bacilli and reduces risk of relapse in paucibacillary disease.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution over the left thorax. He also has new crusted lesions appearing over 3 days, indicating active viral shedding. Tzanck smear is positive. He has no systemic illness. What is the drug of choice?
opts: Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: For immunocompetent adults with herpes zoster, valacyclovir 1 g TDS for 7 days is preferred for better bioavailability (3-5x that of acyclovir). It produces therapeutic plasma levels equivalent to IV acyclovir. Famciclovir 500 mg TDS is an alternative. Foscarnet is reserved for acyclovir-resistant cases in immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with butterfly-shaped erythema over both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640 (homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are elevated. Which complement pathway abnormality is most associated with severe lupus nephritis?
questions.exp: In active SLE with nephritis, both C3 and C4 are consumed due to classic complement pathway activation by immune complexes. Low C3 and low C4 (with elevated CH50) indicate classical pathway consumption and correlate with disease activity. Low C4 alone can indicate C4 null alleles.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male farmer presents with a crusted plaque with central clearing on his cheek. Multiple tiny, hard, black grain-like particles are visible at the surface. KOH shows thick-walled, muriform (sclerotic) cells that are brown (copper pennies). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is caused by dematiaceous fungi, most commonly Fonsecaea pedrosoi. KOH shows pathognomonic muriform cells (Medlar/copper penny bodies) - thick-walled, brown, multiseptate sclerotic cells. The lesion is a warty plaque with black dots (transepidermal elimination).

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless chancre on the glans penis with a non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (rubbery, discrete). VDRL is reactive 1:32. He reports a new sexual partner 3 weeks ago. What is the drug of choice and duration?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 MU IM stat
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the WHO and CDC recommended treatment. Doxycycline is the alternative in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin has emerging resistance in Treponema pallidum.

questions.q: A 60-year-old presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on elbows, knees, and scalp. He has pitting of the fingernails and distal onycholysis. Auspitz sign is positive. He also reports joint pain. Which nail change is most specific for psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: Oil-drop (salmon-patch) discolouration of the nail is most specific for psoriatic arthritis and indicates enthesitis of the distal phalanx. Pitting is common in psoriasis but not specific for arthritis. Onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and oil-drop changes strongly correlate with psoriatic arthritis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions on the face around the nose and mouth. The mother reports rapid spread in the family. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (non-bullous form). Topical mupirocin 2% is the first-line treatment for localised impetigo. It has excellent efficacy against Staphylococci including MRSA. Fusidic acid is an alternative. Systemic antibiotics are needed for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with dermatomyositis develops V-sign erythema on the chest, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and mechanic's hands. She has proximal muscle weakness. Which investigation is the most sensitive for detecting occult malignancy in this setting?
opts: CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with PET scan
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults carries a 15-30% risk of associated malignancy. CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis combined with PET scan has the highest sensitivity for detecting occult malignancies (ovary, lung, breast, gastrointestinal). Anti-Jo-1 is associated with interstitial lung disease, not malignancy. Age/gender-appropriate cancer screening is essential.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with oral erosions preceding cutaneous blisters. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular 'chicken-wire' IgG deposition throughout the epidermis. Anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies are elevated. What is the most appropriate initial systemic treatment?
opts: Rituximab 1 g IV two doses 2 weeks apart
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is the diagnosis. Initial treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day) combined with an adjuvant steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine 2-3 mg/kg/day or mycophenolate mofetil). Rituximab is now considered first-line in some guidelines for moderate-severe PV due to excellent remission rates.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with multiple hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk. Slit-skin smear is negative. Nerve biopsy shows granulomas with epithelioid cells but no AFB. There are fewer than 5 skin lesions. What is the WHO recommended treatment regimen?
opts: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg/day for 6 months
Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg/day + Clofazimine 50 mg/day for 12 months
Single dose rifampicin, ofloxacin, and minocycline (ROM) for a single lesion only
questions.exp: Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy with 2-5 lesions is treated with WHO MDT-PB: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered) for 6 months. Single lesion PB can use ROM regimen. MB leprosy requires a 3-drug regimen for 12 months.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with multiple tender, erythematous nodules on the shins developing over 2 weeks. She also has fever, arthralgia, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. Biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (Löfgren syndrome variant) is a classic presentation of acute sarcoidosis. EN shows septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis on biopsy (vs erythema induratum which shows lobular panniculitis WITH vasculitis, usually associated with TB). Löfgren syndrome has an excellent prognosis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a 4 cm pigmented lesion on the sole with irregular borders, variegated colour, and satellite lesions. Dermoscopy shows parallel ridge pattern. Excision biopsy shows Breslow thickness 3.2 mm, Clark level IV, ulceration present, and 3 mitoses/mm2. What is the T staging?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition melanoma T staging: T3 = Breslow 2.01-4 mm. This lesion at 3.2 mm = T3; with ulceration present it becomes T3b. T4b would require Breslow >4 mm with ulceration.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the corona of the glans penis. It has a clean base with indurated, firm edges. There is no exudate. The patient is from a region where chancroid is endemic. Which test has the highest specificity for syphilis screening?
questions.exp: FTA-ABS is the most specific treponemal test for syphilis (specificity ~99%). VDRL and RPR are non-treponemal tests used for screening and monitoring treatment response; they have false positives. TPHA is also highly specific but FTA-ABS is considered the gold standard confirmatory test.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with intensely itchy erythematous papules and vesicles on the scalp, face, neck folds, and flexures. The mother has a history of atopic dermatitis. IgE levels are markedly elevated. What mutation is most strongly associated with the development of atopic dermatitis?
questions.exp: Loss-of-function mutations in FLG (filaggrin gene) are the strongest genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis. Filaggrin is essential for skin barrier function; mutations lead to increased water loss, allergen penetration, and sensitisation. FLG mutations are present in ~30% of European atopic dermatitis patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery. The surgeon explains the advantages of this technique. Which statement best describes the unique advantage of Mohs surgery over standard wide local excision?
opts: It allows reconstruction of the defect at the same sitting
It examines 100% of the surgical margins intraoperatively using horizontal frozen sections
It uses vertical bread-loaf sections that sample all margins
It reduces recurrence by using wider margins than conventional excision
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery's key advantage is examination of 100% of surgical margins using horizontal (tangential) frozen sections, allowing precise mapping of residual tumour. Standard pathology uses vertical bread-loaf sections that sample only ~1% of the margin. Mohs achieves the highest cure rates for BCC/SCC with maximum tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman taking long-term hydroxychloroquine for SLE presents for routine ophthalmic screening. She complains of reading difficulty. What is the recommended maximum daily dose of hydroxychloroquine to minimise retinal toxicity?
opts: 400 mg/day if BMI <25, 200 mg/day if BMI >30
200 mg/day for all patients after 5 years
questions.exp: Current guidelines (ACR, AAO) recommend hydroxychloroquine at or below 5 mg/kg/day of actual body weight to minimise retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy). Baseline ophthalmology exam at initiation and annual screening after 5 years are recommended.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with perifollicular hyperkeratosis and haemorrhagic follicular papules on the lower limbs. He also has gingival haemorrhage and corkscrew hairs. He is a college student who has been living on instant noodles for 6 months. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Scurvy (Vitamin C/ascorbic acid deficiency) classically presents with perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew/swan-neck hairs, gingival haemorrhage, and impaired wound healing. Vitamin C is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis. Poor diet avoiding fresh fruits and vegetables is the cause.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss 3 months after delivering a baby. Pull test is positive with more than 6 hairs. Trichogram shows >25% telogen hairs. What is the most likely pathophysiology?
opts: Elevated prolactin causing premature catagen entry
Synchronised shift of hair follicles into telogen due to hormonal changes post-partum
Autoimmune attack on hair follicle bulge
Iron deficiency causing anagen hair fragility
questions.exp: Post-partum telogen effluvium occurs 2-5 months after delivery. During pregnancy, elevated oestrogen prolongs the anagen (growth) phase. After delivery, oestrogen drops, causing synchronised entry of hair follicles into telogen, followed by shedding. It is self-limiting and resolves within 6-12 months.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer from Rajasthan presents with verrucous, cauliflower-like tumorous masses on the dorsum of the hand and forearm. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with neutrophilic microabscesses and thick-walled brown fungal elements. What is the most effective treatment for extensive chromoblastomycosis?
opts: Potassium iodide saturated solution (SSKI) for 3 months
questions.exp: Itraconazole 200-400 mg/day is the treatment of choice for chromoblastomycosis. Treatment duration is typically 12-24 months for extensive disease. Terbinafine 500-1000 mg/day is an alternative with comparable efficacy. Combination itraconazole + terbinafine may be used for refractory cases. SSKI is used for sporotrichosis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with violaceous papules on the wrists and oral mucosal white lacy reticulation. Koebner phenomenon is positive. Histopathology shows sawtooth acanthosis, hypergranulosis, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, and civatte bodies. What are civatte bodies?
opts: Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in keratinocytes
Apoptotic keratinocytes in the basal layer that have been expelled into the dermis
Neutrophilic microabscesses in the papillary dermis
Plasma cells forming Russell bodies in the infiltrate
questions.exp: Civatte bodies (colloid/hyaline bodies) in lichen planus are apoptotic keratinocytes, primarily from the basal layer, expelled into the papillary dermis. They appear as eosinophilic, rounded bodies (IgM-positive on DIF). They represent keratinocyte damage from cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-mediated attack at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with a well-defined area of total hair loss on the scalp, 4 cm in diameter, with exclamation mark hairs at the periphery and a positive pull test. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots and black dots. What is the most important prognostic factor for severe/chronic disease?
opts: Atopic diathesis and onset in childhood
Single patch restricted to scalp vertex
questions.exp: In alopecia areata, poor prognostic factors include: childhood onset, atopic diathesis, extensive disease (alopecia totalis/universalis), ophiasis pattern, nail involvement, family history, and Down syndrome. Atopy is associated with more severe and refractory disease. Single scalp patch with short duration has the best prognosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman taking isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne is found to be pregnant. She asks about the teratogenic effects. Which of the following is NOT a recognised teratogenic effect of isotretinoin?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is highly teratogenic. Recognised defects include: CNS (hydrocephalus, microcephaly), ear (microtia, anotia), conotruncal cardiac defects, thymic aplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities. Limb reduction defects are NOT a typical isotretinoin teratogenicity - thalidomide causes limb defects (phocomelia).

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) presents with intensely pruritic papules and urticarial plaques starting on the abdomen with sparing of the umbilicus, spreading to thighs and buttocks. She is in her first pregnancy carrying twins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (also called PEP - polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) is the most common specific dermatosis of pregnancy. It begins in striae on the abdomen, characteristically SPARES the umbilicus, and spreads to thighs. It is more common in primigravidas, multiple pregnancies, and excessive weight gain. DIF is negative. It resolves after delivery.

questions.q: A 45-year-old dark-skinned woman presents with symmetrical brown-black hyperpigmented patches on the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip, worsened by sun exposure. She has been using oral contraceptive pills for 2 years. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of the pigmentation. What layer of skin is primarily affected?
opts: Epidermal (increased melanin in basal and suprabasal keratinocytes)
questions.exp: Melasma has three patterns on Wood's lamp: epidermal (most common) shows enhancement, dermal shows no enhancement, and mixed is intermediate. In epidermal melasma, increased melanin is deposited in basal and suprabasal keratinocytes. Wood's lamp enhancement confirms epidermal pattern, which has the best response to topical depigmenting agents.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a warty, verrucous plaque on the lower leg that has been slowly growing for 10 years. Histopathology shows well-differentiated squamous carcinoma with minimal atypia, pushing rather than infiltrating margins, and areas resembling condyloma acuminatum. HPV types 6 and 11 are detected. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Verrucous carcinoma (Buschke-Lowenstein tumour equivalent on leg)
Squamous cell carcinoma arising in lichen sclerosus
questions.exp: Verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade, well-differentiated SCC variant associated with HPV 6 and 11. It has pushing (not infiltrating) margins on histology. On the lower leg it is called epithelioma cuniculatum; on genitalia (Buschke-Lowenstein tumour); on plantar surface (carcinoma cuniculatum). It rarely metastasises but is locally destructive.

questions.q: A patient with multibacillary leprosy on MDT develops a sudden, painful, erythematous swelling of pre-existing skin lesions, fever, and mild uveitis. Nerve conduction studies show deterioration. This episode occurred 18 months into treatment. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Stop MDT immediately and start prednisolone
Continue MDT and start prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day
Switch to ROM (rifampicin, ofloxacin, minocycline) regimen
questions.exp: This describes Type 1 (reversal) lepra reaction characterised by upgrading inflammation of skin lesions and acute neuritis. The critical rule is to CONTINUE MDT (stopping increases bacillary load and risk of relapse) and add prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day for a minimum of 12-24 weeks to prevent permanent nerve damage. Thalidomide is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions.
